prime.problem: "How long until we've seen every one?" covers test coverage by random inputs, hash buckets all hit, every shard warmed and every sticker collected. Intuition says n draws for n types; the real mean is n·H<sub>n</sub>, 2.45 times as many for a die and growing like n ln n.
prime.fits: It's a total of independent pieces, like the CLT card, but the pieces are cs-8's geometric waits with shrinking success chances. The order-statistics card met the same harmonic numbers in continuous time.
expect: Var(T) as a sum of stage variances
n ln n growth and a right-skewed tail
prime.goal: Split a collect-them-all wait into geometric stages, get its exact mean and variance, predict how it scales with n, and say when the formula no longer applies.

attend: Why does each stage's success chance depend only on how many faces are left, and why does that make the stages independent?
Why does the last stage dominate both the mean (6 of 14.7) and the variance (30 of 38.99)?
Where does the n ln n growth come from, and what does E[T]/n = H<sub>n</sub> mean in words?
What breaks in the stage argument when the die is loaded?

must: Split the wait at each new face → stage k waits for one of the n − k + 1 unseen faces → Geometric(p<sub>k</sub>) with mean 1/p<sub>k</sub> → linearity gives E[T] = Σ n/(n − k + 1) = nH<sub>n</sub> = 14.7 for a die
Each stage's chance depends only on how many faces remain, not on past rolls → stages are independent → their variances add → Var(T) = Σ (1 − p<sub>k</sub>)/p<sub>k</sub>² = 38.99
Late stages have tiny p<sub>k</sub> → long geometric waits → the last stage alone is 6 of 14.7 rolls and 30 of 38.99 variance → T is right-skewed (median 13, P(T > 30) = 0.0252)
H<sub>n</sub> ≈ ln n + 0.5772 → E[T] ≈ n ln n → each new coupon type costs more than the last (235.98 draws for 52 cards)
elevated: Unequal probabilities break fixed stage chances → inclusion–exclusion over the missing set still works → the loaded die needs 1439/63 ≈ 22.84 rolls, dominated by the rare faces

compress.prompt: From memory, write the stage table for a die (p, mean, variance per stage) and the two totals. Add one arrow chain from "fewer faces left" to "right-skewed T".
checklist: variances add because stages are independent → 38.99
the last stage dominates, so T is right-skewed
nH<sub>n</sub> grows like n ln n

retrieve.q: Explain why the stage lengths are independent even though they come from the same sequence of rolls.
answer: a stage's chance of ending on each roll depends only on how many faces are still missing
that count is fixed during the stage, whatever happened before
so each stage is a fresh geometric wait, independent of the others

retrieve.q: Walk through computing E[T] and Var(T) for a four-sided die.
You want the chance of needing more than 30 rolls for a die. Compare the CLT normal approximation with the exact inclusion–exclusion tail: what does each give and why do they differ?
answer: normal with mean 14.7, sd 6.244 and a ½ correction: 1 − Φ((30.5 − 14.7)/6.244) = 0.0057, about 4.4× too small
T is right-skewed (the long last stage), and six stages aren't enough for the CLT to wash that out

compare.q: Each stage here is a geometric wait. What's different about chaining several with changing p, and how does memorylessness make the chaining legal?
answer: one geometric has a fixed p; here p drops as faces are collected
memorylessness means each stage starts fresh at the moment a new face appears
so the total is a sum of independent geometrics with known p's

compare.q: T is a total of independent pieces. Why doesn't the CLT card's recipe give accurate tails here, while it did well for the middle of A.J.'s 20 jobs?
answer: the pieces are not identically distributed: the last few dominate the variance
only 6 pieces, one of which (mean 6, variance 30) is very skewed
the CLT needs many comparable pieces; here the exact inclusion–exclusion tail is the right tool

predict.q: Before computing: for a 12-sided die, is the expected number of rolls closer to 24, 37 or 60? And will E[T]/n be larger or smaller than a six-sided die's 2.45?
predict.answer: About 37: 12 × H<sub>12</sub> = 12 × 3.1032 = 37.24. E[T]/n = H<sub>12</sub> = 3.10 > 2.45: draws per coupon grow like ln n, so each face costs more on average as n grows.

apply.task: Use mean_var for n = 4 and n = 12 and compare with your hand answers. Then use cdf to find P(T > 30) for a six-sided die and compare it with the normal approximation 1 − Φ((30.5 − 14.7)/6.244).
apply.done: You print E = 25/3, Var = 130/9 for n = 4 and E ≈ 37.24 for n = 12, and for the die the exact tail 0.0252 against the normal's 0.0057, and you can say in one sentence why the normal is low.
apply.hint: The normal ignores the right skew from the long last stage.
